title: Lojong - Smoke in the Air
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's talk highlights the importance of accepting reality as it is, rather than trying to change or avoid it. This involves taking responsibility for one's actions, being grateful for everyone and everything, and embracing confusion and imperfection. By doing so, we can cultivate a deeper understanding of reality and awaken to new possibilities, allowing our lives to evolve and transform in response to the challenges we face.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Thanks for coming on this smoky night.
Last Saturday, Bob and I and a few others went up into the mountains and did a ritual hike we've been doing every year for a while.
Usually we do it as a multi-day backpack.
The way the circumstances were this year, we did it as a day hike along this trail, which has become very familiar.
We've gone the same trail every year for many years.
We hike in silence and just try to feel our bodies in the mountain.
We do rituals along the way and chant text from Zen Master Dogen from the 13th century called Mountains and Rivers Sutra, Teaching of the Mountains and Rivers.
I'll stop along the trail, and you've heard of this before, I think, probably. [unclear: "I wasn't here by here one time"], Bob, you mean a talk where you detailed every single thing along the way.
So that's in our archive somewhere.
If you have a few hours, a long drive to Seattle, you can listen to Bob walk you through.
It would be great.
Probably about the right thing.
Yeah, it's great.
And it was really beautiful.
It was a little smoky, but it was okay.
One of the members of the group came over from the other side of the mountains from the Twisp area, and he said it was much, much better where we were and he was glad to be there.
It was long to do this as a day hike, like 17 miles.
Earlier in the summer I had done a few hikes over 15, 20 miles and I really found the last five miles pretty unpleasant, and I vowed never to do that again.
You can do it.
It depends on whatever your limit is.
That's a little bit too much.
But that wasn't the case at all somehow.
Something about doing it together and doing it in silence: we just sort of flowed, and the text talks a lot about water flowing and mountains flowing.
Mountains walking.
So this time the last three or four miles were just like water or wind or something.
It was really peaceful.
So it was a wonderful, long day.
We got back just at dark.
We actually got some pictures this time.
We usually don't get pictures.
One of the pictures that Terrell Thompson got was of me lighting up a flashlight so Bob could sign the little trailhead registry to say we made it out safely.
It just got dark at that moment where you couldn't quite see.
A couple days later I had another trip to the mountains long planned.
I'm really trying to go to the mountains more in the summer.
I'm finding it very nourishing to be outside in the mountains.
This was a trip with my friend Brennan, who you might remember spoke very movingly at the guiding teacher ceremony, if you were here.
Remember that?
Yeah.
He's a really dear friend, and I don't have that many close friends who aren't involved in the sangha or work or something.
So it's good to have friends.
At one point, 10 or 15 years ago, my wife said to me, you've had this conversation too with your wife, "Do you ever see anybody who's not in the sangha?"
I don't know.
I love you all, and that's not healthy.
I only ever see people in the group.
Anyway, Brennan likes hiking too, so we had this trip planned.
The big hike with Bob and everybody was on Saturday, and this was the very next afternoon.
We were going to drive in and camp at the trailhead and then do this big mountain climb on Monday morning.
I was so excited about it.
Then on Sunday afternoon, before he was going to come over, he texts me: are you sure?
All this smoke?
And I'm like, no, no, no, it's fine.
I want to go on this hike.
It's going to be great.
We had a few exchanges like that and I convinced him it'd be fine.
It was just up there yesterday.
It's great.
It's fine.
It's fine.
Well, it turns out things change, and change very rapidly.
We're driving up to Darrington and it's just getting worse and worse.
You can see less and less.
Once we get to Darrington, there's an enormous mountain right above it, White Horse Mountain.
Couldn't see it at all.
So we finally decided, well, we made it all this way, we might as well go to the trailhead.
We got to the trailhead and we thought, well, we might as well day hike to the little lake that's a mile in, where we might camp in the future.
This is a climb called Mount Pug, P-U-G-H.
Never heard of it before.
He looked it up.
There's a million mountains in there.
It's unbelievable what country we live in.
And that proved to be pretty unpleasant.
We're getting headaches and feeling a little nauseous.
We do get to this little lake, and there's a wonderful moment.
We see a pair of owls, barred owls, probably nesting there, and they were fishing in the lake.
That was pretty awesome as we were sitting there panting.
And I just felt more and more upset.
Like, this can't be happening.
How can the air itself betray us, and not be good to breathe?
I worked a little harder than I meant to.
It was last spring and partly this summer, which seems to be my pattern.
I'm trying to do that less, but I'd really envisioned this particular backpack as a really important stress release and getting grounded again.
I didn't realize how much I'd pinned my sanity on my imagination of what was going to happen on this particular hike.
I'd just had a beautiful hike the day before, so I don't know why that didn't work.
You know what I mean?
Somehow this was the hike that was going to reset.
And then I find myself Monday morning on the couch.
The schedule was cleared.
I had nothing to do.
I'm not enjoying myself at all, Googling about air quality and what this particulate matter that's less than 2.5 microns is doing to our lungs, which is what they're measuring.
We have to know these things now.
You can just Google Bellingham air quality and it will very quickly give you a number on a nice, very easy to read chart.
Of course, I could have Googled Darrington air quality and seen that instead.
When we left Bellingham, it was at the last notch on the green, just teetering over the edge.
Meanwhile, Darrington's over here.
And I didn't know that.
There's a million factors in everything.
We know that from science and the Dharma: the causes and conditions that lead to huge forest fires and lots of smoke, and then lead to the smoke being here and not somewhere else.
And what is this wanting the smoke to be somewhere else?
Who is it that we want to send the smoke to?
Out in the ocean, would that be okay?
The whales?
Anyway, there are a lot of factors, but it's pretty darn clear that the climate is changing, partly as a result of our activities.
At first they called this global warming, and then realized it's a lot more complicated than just everything getting warmer.
Some things might get colder, and then people will say, well, it's not global warming, look, it's getting colder there, but it's hotter there.
So then they decided to call it climate change.
But of course, there's absolutely no question that on the whole the Earth is getting warmer.
We're having the warmest year on record year after year, and these hotter, drier conditions make fires more intense.
I was talking a little bit to a friend who hangs out with wilderness firefighters.
They're saying that the quality of the fires is different.
The way they move is different.
The way they jump from tree to tree is different.
It's a whole different kind of thing.
So anyway, I was sitting there on Monday morning, just really feeling sad and depressed and hopeless.
The climate change kind of came home in a certain way, because I drove to Darrington in the smoke and had an unpleasant day hike and had to turn around and drive back.
I didn't get what I wanted on that day, because it actually affected me directly and experientially.
And I couldn't do what I wanted.
So I was thinking about learning and change.
Maybe all real learning has to be in some way experiential like that.
It can't just be an idea that we read about or a conversation we have, although that's a certain kind of learning and true enough in its way.
But anyways, I was remembering I took a class in environmental science in 1985 in college, and the characteristics of CO2 and the greenhouse gas effects and all that were well known then.
Then they were more worried about the ozone layer being destroyed.
Remember that?
From oxygen-free radicals.
I forgot to remind myself of the chemistry, but it's all pretty simple chemistry actually.
Well understood.
This stuff's not complicated.
But we in large part solved that problem.
The ozone hole shrank again, partly because we banned some really stupid chemicals, and succeeded in that.
So it's not like we can't reverse things.
But 33 years later here we are, the planet's on fire and just getting hotter.
So it really shook me up.
I don't want to depress you.
You need to be shook up in your own way, not by me.
But maybe we all need to be shook up in some way, and understand that our actions matter.
We were doing a little study earlier, one of the groups, and we were looking at the idea of renunciation.
That practice involves joyfully letting go, joyfully renouncing things for the good of beings, for compassion's sake.
My wife is telling me it's time that we should renounce air travel.
And she's probably right.
She's probably right.
And that's hard to do, right?
I really had a good time in Costa Rica.
It was cool.
But I'm part of why there's smoke in the air.
And maybe you are too.
So eventually I realized I just had to get out of the house even though it was smoky.
My wife had the good suggestion: well, stay low.
Maybe better low.
So I went down to the Skagit River and Fir Island and sat by the river.
Found a little public access spot.
It didn't really say no camping, so I camped there.
Nobody noticed.
I just had to be somewhere overnight and outside.
I later looked up the number, and the number in the Skagit Valley wasn't really that much better than the number in Darrington.
But I didn't hike too hard and just took it easy, and so I came to feel better.
I came to remember that it's also still a beautiful world full of wise and resilient people.
We've been talking about compassion this year, and I was remembering that in the introduction to Norman Fischer's book, Training in Compassion, he does mention ecological disasters.
So I'm like, okay, here's an ecological disaster that's happening right now in real time.
How can we study compassion here?
I'm going to let Norman help us, because I just didn't have the wherewithal to think of a brilliant way to approach this.
I thought I'd read a few pages of the introduction to the book, which maybe you've read before, but it bears repeating.
And we can look at a few of the compassion training slogans and maybe how I or we might apply them in this case.
So Norman wrote:
*Times are tough.
We live fast paced lives with considerable political, economic and ecological upheaval.*
And you're like, how do you know?

*And the resultant dread, fear and stress makes life difficult for almost everyone, except possibly for those who opt for self-defensive denial, which only defers the pain and probably makes it worse.
But times have always been tough.
Living a human life in a human world on a limited planet has always been a daunting proposition.
Circling the wagons, assuming a self-centered defensive stance has never been successful, never been a successful coping mechanism, natural though the impulse may be.
We are programmed by evolution also in the opposite way.
We are cooperating animals, deeply conditioned to be concerned for one another.*
*Our hearts are also made for loving.
Compassion and connection not only feels good and right, as all of our religious traditions teach us, but also turns difficulties into opportunities.
As we have so often seen, when in the course of the seemingly more frequent natural disasters of recent years, neighbors go out of their way to help one another.
When they do, tragedy can become inspirational.
Paradoxically, life can seem more rather than less meaningful when our world is suddenly shattered.
When we are a witness to genuine compassion in the face of great suffering, we seem to transcend our difficulties.*
*When we feel like helping, we do help and we are helped.
We become stronger, happier, and more resilient people.
Compassion and resilience are not, as we might imagine, rarefied human qualities available only to the saintly.
Nor are they adventitious experiences that arise in us only in extraordinary special circumstances.
In fact, these essential and universally prized human qualities can be solidly cultivated by anyone willing to take the time to do it.
They can become the way we are and live on a daily basis.
We can train our minds.
We are not stuck with our fearful, self-centered ways of seeing and feeling.
And mind, as I mean it in this book, is more than just the intellect.*
This is important.
*Mind is more than just the intellect.
It also includes sensations, emotions, subtle senses of subjectivity, desires, aspirations, attitudes, images, concepts, perceptions, and so on.
In a word, mind is consciousness, the sum total of all of our human experience.
In this sense, mind completely includes the body.
We are conscious of our bodily sensations and our emotions.
Our thoughts, too, affect us bodily and vice versa.
Most of us think of our minds the way we are, our basic attitudes and reactions, as being fixed.
Fixed by our genetic inheritance and our life experience.
We assume that our basic feelings and reactions are simply a given, indelibly fixed in us.*
*We can learn information and specific skills, which is why we go to school, or invest in training programs.
Yet we may believe that our basic character remains the same.
For genetically or environmentally programmed to be angry, sad, depressed, or cheerful people will continue to be that way, more or less throughout our lives.
We are who we are.*
So it's interesting reflecting on that, isn't it?
It's probably part of you that says, no, no, I can change, and part of you says, that's right, I am who I am.
Maybe it's kind of both.
So it goes on to introduce the system from Tibetan Buddhism, which is so helpful, even in this contemporary situation.
All these things were created thousands of years ago.
The text of Dogen's we were reading, Bob was amazed to remember, was written 800 years ago.
This system of training was created longer ago than that, a thousand years ago.
It's a training where you use simple phrases, slogans, to remind you of deep truths and to help you work with them.
We have to work with these things, kind of like somehow being out in the smoke helped me work with, not denying climate change, not holding it at arm's length.
I've even been kind of cheerfully telling people, yeah, well, the Pacific Northwest is the best place to be.
Our climate is just going to get a little nicer.
It's embarrassing, when I thought that.
The slogans are arranged in several sections, and I want to talk about the section that seems most important to me, a section called "transform bad circumstances into the path."
This, we must admit, is a bad circumstance.
You're full of smoke.
One of the news reports said, just hanging around outside, or maybe it was being outside or being active, I'm not sure, yesterday it was like you smoked seven cigarettes.
That's kind of frightening, right?
So here are the slogans within this section, this point of transform bad circumstances into the path.
I wonder if one of these speaks to you.
You might try taking it up in your life.
I wasn't thorough enough to figure out whether any of our excellent speakers, while I was away, spoke on these.
But the great news about Dharma talks, for those of you who give them, is that it always bears repeating, so you can't go wrong.
Besides, people have been repeating these 57 slogans for more than a thousand years.
The first point is turn all mishaps into the path.
Turn all mishaps into the path.
See a problem as part of your path.
Next is drive all blames into one.
Drive all blames into one.
Something about blame matters, paying attention to blame.
Next is be grateful to everyone.
And it actually does say be grateful to everyone.
It doesn't say be grateful to pretty much everyone.
Grateful to everyone.
Then it says see confusion as Buddha and practice emptiness.
It requires some unpacking, and this is one of those where Norman messed with the traditional phrasing.
This is good though.
See confusion as Buddha and practice emptiness.
Next is do good, avoid evil, appreciate your lunacy, and pray for help.
Maybe that says everything I'm trying to say tonight.
Do good, avoid evil, appreciate your lunacy, pray for help.
The last one kind of goes back to the first.
Whatever you meet is the path.
Whatever you meet is the path.
This is all in a way pretty clear, but not so easy, because we have some deeply persistent views that things should be other than the way they are.
The Buddha decided this was the first point that he wanted to bring up when he started teaching.
And pretty much that's all he taught for 30-whatever years.
We have this persistent desire for things to be other than the way they are.
And if we persist in that view, what happens?
We suffer.
We suffer.
So we need another way than just wishing something was some other way.
And of course the way this manifests, this wishing things are other than the way they are, is often quite sophisticated, right?
All kinds of clever ways that we try to avoid things, or change the subject, or complain, as if that could make things better.
Not that we don't want to change and improve everything, but we have to start.
These teachings suggest that the only way we'll ever be of any modicum of happiness and effectiveness both is if we start by deeply accepting what is.
And then, that's why the metaphor of the path is so helpful, and then take the next step.
But if we can't accept where we're standing, what will happen?
We'll never be grounded, right?
We'll never be stable.
If we can't accept where we're standing, we can't walk, right?
We're only balancing on one foot the whole time.
So, turning all mishaps into the path: I don't know how exactly to apply these to climate change.
I'm just working this through myself.
But it seems like there's been some big mishaps here.
How is this a path?
So this is a question.
I don't know if there's a clear answer.
We can certainly educate ourselves more.
We can certainly take small steps.
Burning at least a little less fossil fuel matters, right?
We can be willing to depress people by bringing these things up in talks.
But to not see it as either to be avoided or to be overwhelmed by, but path means a step.
To turn all mishaps into taking a step.
So what's the next step?
And this all happened through accumulation of many, many decisions made by many people, right?
So although there are very large forces at play that are much bigger than you or I, that are very distressing and overwhelming, also everything changes and everything is affected by everything we do.
Maybe it's being politically more active.
Many of us have been trying to do that in various ways for the last year and a half, right?
So, turn all mishaps into the path.
It's also helpful to not think of these as something that I need an answer to right now or I don't get it and there's no point.
But to have these touchstones, to have these in your back pocket, to have these beneath your pillow, to turn them over every day.
How can I turn this mishap into the path?
And maybe we start with smaller things than global climate catastrophes, too.
How can I turn my grouchiness into the path?
How can I turn my impatience into the path?
How can I turn my confusion into the path?
Second slogan in this section is drive all blames into one.
This is taking responsibility, full responsibility.
There are other people who have done horrible things, to be sure.
This is not absolving anyone of their responsibility, but also recognizing that we're all responsible and that we're responsible together.
No matter what you think about political parties or however things should or shouldn't be, we all participated in creating the situation we have now.
So how can I take full responsibility and stop blaming everybody else?
Drive all blames into one.
Next is be grateful to everyone.
This whole thing is a powerful practice and a kind of holding opposites.
It's not so easy for a mind, right?
We have a mind that wants it to be this way or that way, right?
People are this way or they're that way.
It's a disaster or it's not a problem, right?
So the first section I just mentioned, in this slogan be grateful to everyone, is also to open our eyes and see the beauty that's all around us and within us.
Our incredible intelligence and wisdom and love, our unbelievable creativity and our ridiculous, dogged...
What's the word I want?
Perspicastic?
There's some word I want, but I can't come up with it.
You know the word I want.
But you know what I mean?
We just keep going.
We're amazing.
So be grateful that everyone is here going with us and helping us.
And remember that it's a self-centered conceit to think that I alone am me and I made all this that's my life.
I didn't create my life.
A million gazillion people helped to create my life with me and for me.
And I can be grateful to every one of them, those that I know and those that I don't know.
When I was thinking about taking that [unclear: "Murmell Sciences"] class in 1985, I was remembering the professor was a guy named Jim Pepper.
He was just so cheerful and energetic, and he had just gotten new glasses, like bifocals.
They made him look around like this, and he said, "I'm like a bird."
Now that I remember his name and that he said that, 30-whatever years ago, I'm grateful to Jim Pepper.
I'm grateful to so many people, aren't you?
There's so much to be grateful for.
And not just people.
Sitting there on that lake and watching the incredibly silent flight of the owls.
We're not even that.
Just so grateful.
So beautiful.
How could nature, God, evolution, whatever forces have manifested that?
An owl.
Unbelievable.
Literally unbelievable.
Be grateful to everyone and everything.
If we're not grateful, we're really stuck.
Next is see confusion as Buddha and practice emptiness.
We can't have awakening without confusion.
So, to be grateful also to our confusion, to our limited views, to our anger, to our blaming and complaining, because these are the tools of awakening.
These help us to see.
Sometimes it takes a while.
We're stubborn.
These help us to wake up.
So even our confusion and problems, our awakening, our Buddha are helping us.
We still have to show up.
We still have to practice.
It doesn't happen automatically.
Practice is not a way to go on autopilot with really good tools.
To see our confusion as Buddha means to practice with our confusion.
To be awakened and awakening in our confusion.
See confusion as Buddha and practice emptiness.
Practice emptiness means understand that it's not the way we think it is exactly.
There's more that we don't see yet.
We're only seeing the surface.
The depth is empty and unknown to us and interconnected with other things in ways we can't understand.
And it's all much more fluid and changeable and changing.
It's not monolithic.
It's empty of this kind of solidity that we put on it, as are we.
That's why we can train our minds.
It's because of emptiness.
If it weren't for emptiness we really would be fixed in our position with our personality and our habits and our quirks.
We change because we're empty of that fixed identity.
We just made it up.
A lot of people helped us make it up.
I'm grateful to them too.
Thank you for helping me make up me, but it's just a made up story.
And it can change.
Two more.
Do good, avoid evil, appreciate your lunacy, pray for help.
So it actually doesn't matter what we do.
This is precepts.
Do good.
Drive less, whatever it is.
Do good.
Avoid evil.
One great way, and this is from Norman too, I think, or who knows where he got it, one way to describe good and evil is: good is action that increases awareness.
Evil is action that increases suffering.
Even a little bit.
Trash talking somebody increases suffering.
Do good, avoid evil.
Appreciate your lunacy.
It's kind of the same as see confusion as Buddha.
And that's one of the great things about sangha life.
We can appreciate each other's lunacy.
What a bunch of kooks, right?
And isn't it wonderful to be a little more honest about that?
Not have to have this... a little bit less, a little bit less, we're still burdened by it.
A little less of the burden of trying to be like, "I have it together.
I'm a grown up.
I got it together.
I know what to do."
Of course we don't, because we're basically insane, in the good way.
Lunacy is the moon, right?
Luna.
So be moon-like, too.
Pray for help.

We don't usually use the word prayer in Buddhism, so maybe you can say hope for help if you don't like the word prayer, but the great thing about prayer, or whatever you want to call it, is to call forth something bigger than my personal idea of me.
To call on Buddha, Kuan Yin, Kanzeon, Namu, Butsue.
To call upon God, to call upon all our relations, to call upon the great Earth, to call upon Mother Nature, to call upon all beings.
This is prayer.
And it opens us up.
It releases us from some of our less helpful lunacy.
It softens our self-centeredness.
And it helps us be humble.
The first thing we need to do is be humble through all this, right?
And then last, we go back to the beginning.
Whatever you meet is the path.
This is hard to practice when you meet it sometimes.
You meet something that you do not love.
There's a line from Rumi that's something like, be grateful for everything that comes.
Even if... how does the line go exactly?
*Be grateful for whoever comes.
Even if they are like a demon, clearing your house, smashing your house of all its furniture, still he or she may be clearing you out for some new delight.*
So be grateful for the disasters in your life.
They may be clearing you out for some new delight.
And who hasn't had times in your life where something was going terribly wrong and it was the worst thing ever, and then somehow on the back side of it, there was something new?
Some new vision, a new door opened.
Not always, right?
Sometimes you just suffer, and that's your path.
To suffer.
Thich Nhat Hanh gets portrayed as a very sweet kind of teacher, but one of the things I love about him is he teaches this great essay I read once.
He said, the important thing in life, and you're like, yeah, what's it going to be?
The important thing in life is to learn how to suffer well.
Learn how to suffer well.
So that's whatever you meet as the path.
None of this is easy or clear, exactly.
But these are powerful tools, I think, to help us to face what's hard to face, whether weather...
I'm not saying that climate change can be a number of things.
It does seem to learn and understand we need to actually go through experiences, we need to get out there, in whatever way getting out there is for you.
But then to get out there with these powerful touchstones in your pocket.

Not just habitual view, not just how I always think about things, not just what I've come to think and believe, but also these as touchstones, little mirrors maybe, little lenses, another way to see things.
I'm grateful for simple lenses.
I don't think I'll be able to read anymore.
So turn all mishaps into the path.
Drive all blames into one.
Be grateful to everyone.
See confusion as Buddha and practice emptiness.
Do good, avoid evil.
Appreciate your lunacy.
Pray for help.
Whatever you meet is the path.
Now just to touch in on a couple brief good things, I want to go back to earlier, where collectively we've been doing some good.
We successfully raised enough money to fund Danetta Okumu's next semester in college in Kenya.
I sent that off through mobile money transfer.
She and her sister, Mercy, were quite delighted.
I asked her to send pictures, so we want to know what school looks like in Kenya.
One of these relatives is like, "Send pictures, Sean.
Send a thank you note."
Hopefully she'll send some pictures.
If you don't know about this, I can give you the back story later.
Also the Family Promise program: we had a tremendous turnout, I think like nine or ten of us, at the training session at First Congregational Church of Bellingham.
FCCB, I learned a new acronym.
They kept saying, "FCCB, FCCB."
I'm like, what are you talking about?
Oh, it's an acronym for the church.
Anyway, it's a program that will be involved in helping homeless families get back on their feet.
It's an interfaith project too, so it's fun we're hanging out with the Christians.
The Christians are hanging out with us and trying to figure out what to call us.
That's cute.
"You're the Zen who?
The Zen what?"
Can I just say you guys?
I'm going to close with a quote from Dogen.
Dogen said one time, and his student wrote this down:
*An ancient one has said, associating with a good teacher is like walking through mist and dew.
Though you will not become drenched, gradually your robe will become damp.*
Associating with a good teacher, or you could translate it as a good person or a good companion,
*associating with a good companion on the way is like walking through mist and dew.
Though you will not become drenched, gradually your robes will become damp.*
So gradually we will wake up.
Suzuki Roshi quotes this too, and I think in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, but I thought you'd be interested to know it came straight from Dogen.
It's in the Zuimonki text.
So thanks for listening to all that.
We appreciate your attention very much.

verbatim.text: Good evening everybody. Thanks for coming on this smoky night. Well, last Saturday, Bob and I and so a few others went up into the mountains and did a ritual hike we've been doing every year for a while. Usually we do it as a multi-day backpack. Just the way the circumstances were this year, we did it as a day hike where we hiked along this trail which has become very familiar. We've gone the same trail every year for several years, many years. And we hike in silence and just try to feel our bodies in the mountain. And then we're doing rituals along the way and chanting text from Zen Master Dogen from the 13th century called Mountains and Rivers Sutra, Teaching of the Mountains and Rivers. I'll stop along the trail and you've heard of this before, I think probably. I wasn't here by here one time, Bob, you mean a talk where you detailed every single thing along the way. So that's in our archive somewhere. If you have a few hours, a long drive to Seattle, you can listen to Bob walk you through, it would be great. Probably about the right thing. Yeah, it's great. And it was really beautiful. It was a little smoky, but it was okay. And one of the members of the group came over from the other side of the mountains from the twist area and he said it was much, much better where we were and he was glad to be there.
